title: Ezra 5:6–17
context: Ezra 5:6–17 gives the text of Tattenai’s letter to Darius. The officials report that the house of the great God is being built with great stones and timber and that the work is going well. They record the elders’ answer: they are servants of the God of heaven and earth, rebuilding the house a great king of Israel built long ago, which was destroyed because their fathers provoked God to wrath. Cyrus decreed its rebuilding in his first year, returned the temple vessels, and entrusted them to Sheshbazzar, who laid the foundations. The officials ask the king to search the royal archives in Babylon to confirm the decree. The letter’s account of Sheshbazzar laying the foundations (5:16) stands alongside Ezra 3:8–10, which describes the foundation laid under Zerubbabel and Jeshua; these notes name the two notices without harmonizing them. Both traditions read the elders’ confession as shared ground: the exile was God’s just judgment, and the rebuilding rests on God’s mercy working through a pagan king’s decree.

verses.text: The copy of the letter that Tattenai, the governor beyond the River, and Shetharbozenai, and his companions the Apharsachites who were beyond the River, sent to Darius the king follows.
verses.arminianNotes: The letter Tattenai, Shetharbozenai, and their companions send to Darius is introduced. Arminians see the inquiry moving to the highest level of Persian government, where God’s purposes will be confirmed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the official record serving God’s plan. Both traditions read the verse as introducing a letter that, despite its purpose, preserves the elders’ testimony about God’s work.

verses.text: They sent a letter to him, in which was written: To Darius the king, all peace.
verses.arminianNotes: The letter opens with a greeting of peace to King Darius. Arminian readers see a formal and respectful report rather than an accusation, which differs from the hostile letter in Ezra 4.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the official style of the letter. Both traditions read the verse as part of a fair report that God would use to confirm the right of the Jews to rebuild.

verses.text: Be it known to the king that we went into the province of Judah, to the house of the great God, which is being built with great stones and timber is laid in the walls. This work goes on with diligence and prospers in their hands.
verses.arminianNotes: The officials report that the house of the great God is being built with great stones and timber, and that the work is going on with diligence and prospering. Arminians see even outsiders recognizing the people’s diligence and success.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the prosperity of the work as God’s blessing. Both traditions note that the officials call him the great God, and they read the verse as an outside witness to the work.

verses.text: Then we asked those elders, and said to them thus, “Who gave you a decree to build this house, and to finish this wall?”
verses.arminianNotes: The officials report that they asked the elders who gave them authority to build the house and finish the wall. Arminian readers see the letter repeating the question of 5:3, setting up the elders’ answer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as part of the formal report. Both traditions see the question as giving the elders an opportunity to testify about God and his works.

verses.text: We asked them their names also, to inform you that we might write the names of the men who were at their head.
verses.arminianNotes: They asked the leaders’ names so they could write them for the king. Arminians see the elders willing to be named, which shows their confidence in the rightness of their work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as an administrative detail. Both traditions see it as preparing for the elders’ answer, which begins by identifying them as servants of God.

verses.text: Thus they returned us answer, saying, “We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth and are building the house that was built these many years ago, which a great king of Israel built and finished.
verses.arminianNotes: The elders answer that they are servants of the God of heaven and earth, rebuilding the house a great king of Israel built long ago. Arminian readers see a clear confession of faith before foreign officials, identifying themselves first by their service to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the confession of God as Lord of heaven and earth, greater than any earthly king. Both traditions note the reference to Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6) and read the verse as shared ground.

verses.text: But after our fathers had provoked the God of heaven to wrath, he gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean, who destroyed this house and carried the people away into Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes: They explain that their fathers provoked the God of heaven to wrath, so he gave them into Nebuchadnezzar’s hand, who destroyed the house and carried the people to Babylon. Arminians see an honest acknowledgment that the exile was the result of their fathers’ sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the confession of God’s sovereign judgment through Nebuchadnezzar. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: the exile was God’s just response to unfaithfulness, not a sign that he was weak.

verses.text: But in the first year of Cyrus king of Babylon, Cyrus the king made a decree to build this house of God.
verses.arminianNotes: In his first year Cyrus king of Babylon decreed that the house of God be rebuilt. Arminian readers see God’s mercy following judgment, and they recall the decree recorded in Ezra 1:1–4.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God moving Cyrus’s heart, as Ezra 1:1 says. Both traditions read the verse as testimony that God’s purpose to restore his people was carried out through a foreign king.

verses.text: The gold and silver vessels of God’s house, which Nebuchadnezzar took out of the temple that was in Jerusalem and brought into the temple of Babylon, those Cyrus the king also took out of the temple of Babylon, and they were delivered to one whose name was Sheshbazzar, whom he had made governor.
verses.arminianNotes: Cyrus took the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had carried to Babylon and gave them to Sheshbazzar, whom he made governor. Arminians see the return of the vessels as a sign that God’s worship was being restored.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and recall Ezra 1:7–11, which lists the vessels. Both traditions read the verse as showing God’s faithfulness in preserving what belonged to his house through the exile.

verses.text: He said to him, ‘Take these vessels, go, put them in the temple that is in Jerusalem, and let God’s house be built in its place.’
verses.arminianNotes: Cyrus told Sheshbazzar to take the vessels to the temple in Jerusalem and to rebuild God’s house on its site. Arminian readers see a clear royal command that the elders now cite as their authority.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s providence securing official permission for the work. Both traditions read the verse as part of the elders’ answer to the question of who authorized the building.

verses.text: Then the same Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundations of God’s house which is in Jerusalem. Since that time even until now it has been being built, and yet it is not completed.
verses.arminianNotes: Sheshbazzar laid the foundations, and the building has continued since then but is not finished. Arminians note that Ezra 3:8–10 describes the foundation laid under Zerubbabel and Jeshua, and they name the two notices without harmonizing them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and leave the relationship between the notices as it stands. Both traditions read the verse as the elders’ honest account that the work began long ago and remained unfinished.

verses.text: Now therefore, if it seems good to the king, let a search be made in the king’s treasure house, which is there at Babylon, whether it is so that a decree was made by Cyrus the king to build this house of God at Jerusalem; and let the king send his pleasure to us concerning this matter.”
verses.arminianNotes: The officials ask the king to search the royal treasure house in Babylon to confirm Cyrus’s decree and to send his decision. Arminian readers see a fair request that allows the truth to be established through proper channels.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God using the search to confirm his people’s right to build. Both traditions read the verse as leading to the discovery of the decree in the next chapter.
